title: Arithmetic Progressions — Chapter Summary
intro: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a sequence in which each term differs from the previous one by a fixed amount called the common difference. This chapter develops the AP definition, derives the n-th-term formula a_n = a + (n − 1) d, derives two equivalent forms for the sum of the first n terms, studies the arithmetic mean of two numbers, and applies APs to short word problems.

sections.heading: Sequences and series
bullets: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers a_1, a_2, a_3, … and may be finite or infinite.
A series is the sum of the terms of a sequence; S_n is the partial sum of the first n terms.
Sequences may be defined by a closed-form rule (a_n = 2 n) or recursively (Fibonacci: a_n = a_(n−1) + a_(n−2)).
Special sequences include the constant, alternating, and Fibonacci sequences.
This chapter focuses on the simplest sequence: one in which successive terms differ by a constant.

sections.heading: Arithmetic progression — definition
bullets: An AP is a sequence with a_2 − a_1 = a_3 − a_2 = … = d, a constant called the common difference.
Given the first term a and common difference d, the AP is a, a + d, a + 2 d, a + 3 d, ….
d > 0: increasing AP; d < 0: decreasing AP; d = 0: constant sequence (still an AP).
To check whether a sequence is an AP, compute successive differences and verify they agree.

sections.heading: n-th term of an AP
bullets: Workhorse formula: a_n = a + (n − 1) d.
Used to find a specific term, the first term given two terms, or the position of a known term.
Find which term equals 205 in 7, 13, 19, …: solve 7 + 6 (n − 1) = 205 → n = 34.
Three-digit multiples of 7: AP 105, 112, …, 994 → 128 terms.

sections.heading: Sum of n terms
bullets: Two equivalent formulae: S_n = (n/2)(2 a + (n − 1) d) = (n/2)(a + l), where l = a_n.
Derived by writing the sum forwards and backwards (Gauss's pairing trick).
Use the first form when only a, d, n are known; use the second when a and l are known.
Standard particular sums: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2; 1 + 3 + … + (2 n − 1) = n^2.
Recover a_n from S_n via a_n = S_n − S_(n−1) (and a_1 = S_1).

sections.heading: Arithmetic mean
bullets: The AM of two numbers a, b is (a + b)/2.
Three numbers x, m, y are in AP iff m = (x + y)/2 — i.e. the middle is the AM of the outer two.
Inserting n arithmetic means between a and b builds an (n + 2)-term AP a, m_1, …, m_n, b with d = (b − a)/(n + 1).
Example: insert 3 AMs between 4 and 24 → d = 5 → 9, 14, 19.
AMs are widely used in averaging two readings, estimating midpoints, and equal-step interpolation.

sections.heading: Word problems
bullets: Four-step recipe: identify the AP, read off a and d (or l), pick the right formula, solve and reject impossible n.
Savings: ₹100, ₹125, ₹150, … → 12th-month saving = ₹375; total in 12 months = ₹2850.
Ladder rungs: 25 rungs from 50 cm down to 25 cm in AP → total length 937.5 cm.
Theatre seating: 30 rows starting at 20 seats with d = 2 → 1470 seats.
Always reject non-natural-number values of n (you can't have 7.4 instalments).

key_takeaways: An AP is a sequence with constant successive differences d.
Sum of n terms: S_n = (n/2)(2 a + (n − 1) d) = (n/2)(a + l).
Three numbers are in AP iff the middle is the arithmetic mean of the other two; insert n means with d = (b − a)/(n + 1).
AP word problems: identify a and d, choose between a_n and S_n, solve, and reject any non-natural n.

glossary.definition: An ordered list of numbers a_1, a_2, a_3, …, finite or infinite.
The sum of the terms of a sequence; S_n denotes the partial sum of the first n terms.
A sequence in which the difference between any two consecutive terms is a fixed constant d.
The constant d = a_(n+1) − a_n that defines an AP.
The first member a (or a_1) of a sequence; for an AP, the AP is a, a + d, a + 2 d, ….
The closed-form expression a_n = a + (n − 1) d for the n-th term of the AP a, a + d, a + 2 d, ….
S_n = (n/2)(2 a + (n − 1) d) = (n/2)(a + l), the sum of the first n terms.
When an AP has n terms, l = a_n = a + (n − 1) d denotes the last term.
The arithmetic mean of two numbers a, b is AM = (a + b)/2; three numbers x, m, y are in AP iff m = (x + y)/2.
Choosing n numbers between a and b so that a, m_1, …, m_n, b is an AP; the common difference is (b − a)/(n + 1).
An AP with d > 0; each term is larger than the previous.
An AP with d < 0; each term is smaller than the previous.
Defining a sequence by giving a_1 (and possibly a_2) and a rule for a_n in terms of earlier terms; e.g. Fibonacci.
